questions.question: Define a magnetic field and compare it with the electric and gravitational fields — what does each act on, and which can repel?
questions.expected_answer: A magnetic field is a region in space where another magnet or ferromagnetic material experiences a force. An electric field is a region where a charge experiences an electric force; a gravitational field is a region where a mass experiences a gravitational force. All three act without contact. Gravity only attracts; electric and magnetic fields can attract or repel. Electric charges can exist singly, but magnetic poles only ever come in north-south pairs.

questions.question: Explain, using domains, why cutting a bar magnet in half always produces two complete magnets and never an isolated pole.
questions.expected_answer: Magnetism comes from the tiny magnetic fields of moving electrons, aligned across regions called domains that all point the same way in a magnet. The poles are just the two ends of this alignment, not separate substances. Any cut produces two shorter aligned pieces, each still with two ends — a north and a south at the cut faces. Hence a magnetic monopole has never been found in nature.

questions.question: State the four rules for drawing magnetic field lines, and describe the field pattern of a bar magnet and of two like poles facing each other.
questions.expected_answer: Rules: lines run from north to south outside the magnet with arrows showing direction; closer spacing means a stronger field (densest at the poles); lines never cross; the field is three-dimensional though drawn flat. Bar magnet: lines fan out from the north pole, arc through space and converge into the south pole. Two like poles facing: the lines bend sharply away from each other, leaving a neutral point between the poles — the picture of repulsion.
